catalog_quote: Basic word stress. In every word of more than one syllable, one of the syllables bears heavy stress ... The location of the heavy stress (whether on the last syllable, the next-to-last, or one of the earlier syllables) is not predictable in Pashto, and the spelling system does not mark stress at all. To ascertain where the heavy stress is in a Pashto word, the non-native speaker must ask a native speaker how to pronounce the word, and then listen for the stressed syllable. The stress in native Pashto words is generally on the last syllable if the syllable ends in a consonant, and on the next-to-last (penultimate) syllable if the last syllable ends in a vowel ... There are probably as many exceptions to the rule given above as there are words which follow it, however, including the word for the language: 'Pashto' ... (2) Deciding source is a 1996 reference grammar by a native-speaker linguist with an explicit stress section; the newer 530-pp Mouton grammar (David 2014, held under sout2649) states 'Word stress in Pashto is assigned lexically' (p.15) and gives stress-only minimal pairs, so the two best modern descriptions agree on lexical. sources.quote: 'Three degrees of stress are found in Pashto: strong, medium and weak. Strong stress is comparatively free, in that it can occur on any syllable of a word, but it is mainly restricted to the first, last or penultimate syllables. It can also, particularly in verbal [inflection], be mobile ... [prewatə́l] to fell / [préwatəl] they fell. Occasionally lexical items may be distinguished solely by stress e.g. [áspa] Mare / [aspá] a disease' (citing Comrie 1987:137); conclusion p.86: 'Stress is used to distinguish similar words having different meanings and is mostly lexical.'
